script.title: How a 2,000-Year-Old Computer Was Found in a Greek Shipwreck
sentences: In 1901, divers pulled a corroded bronze lump from a Greek shipwreck.
For two years, museum staff in Athens ignored it to clean marble statues.
In 1902, archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gear wheel embedded inside the crust.
Scholars dismissed it, convinced gearwork that complex was impossible for the ancient world.
X-ray scans later revealed thirty interlocking bronze gears inside.
It was an analogue computer built in the second century BC to predict eclipses.
Technology of that complexity would not appear again for another fourteen hundred years.
script.description: In 1901, divers discovered a corroded bronze lump in a Greek shipwreck. It turned out to be an ancient analogue computer built over two thousand years ago.

claims_en: Sponge divers retrieved a corroded bronze lump from a Greek shipwreck off Antikythera in 1901.
Museum staff in Athens left the object unnoticed for two years while restoring statues.
In 1902, archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gear wheel embedded in one of the corroded fragments.
Scholars initially considered the device too complex to have been built in the ancient period.
X-ray scans revealed 30 visible meshing bronze gears inside the mechanism fragments.
The Antikythera mechanism was an analogue computer built in the 2nd century BC to predict astronomical positions and eclipses.
Machines of similar complexity did not appear again until 14th-century Western Europe.
